etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 手(て)洗(あら)い (tearai, “hand washing”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 萬 (MC mjonH). Compare modern Cantonese 萬 /万 (maan⁶), Hokkien 萬 /万 (bān).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 萬 (MC mjonH). Compare modern Hokkien 萬 /万 (bān).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨yo₂ro₂du⟩ → */jərədu/ → /jorod͡zu/ → /jorozu/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Appears to be a compound or inflection, but the derivation is unclear. Possibly related to Korean 여러 (yeoreo, “several, various”), in which case the final /-du/ in the Old Japanese might be a voiced version of the generic numeral nominalizer つ (tsu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The ablaut form of 三 (mi, “three”), which it doubles. From Old Japanese 六 (mu), from Proto-Japonic *mu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 六 (MC ljuwk). Compare modern Cantonese 六 (luk⁶), literary Hokkien 六 (lio̍k).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *utui. Doublet of 家(うち) (uchi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 內 (MC nwojH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/mape/ → /mafe/ → /mae/
From Old Japanese as a compound of 目 (ma, “eye”) + 方 (pe₁, “direction, -wards”). Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mapia.
/mape₁/ → /maɸe/ → /mawe/ → /maje/ → /mae/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 前 (MC dzen). Compare modern Mandarin 前 (qián).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Contraction of 御(ご)前(ぜ) (goze), itself a contraction of 御(ご)前(ぜん) (go-zen), an honorific form of address.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Doublet of 務(つと)める (tsutomeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Chinese 醫者 /医者 (yīzhě).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: May originally have been an onomatopoeia. Compare ふうふう (fūfū, “to blow with one's lips rounded”) .

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Considered to be a shift from 四日(よか) (yoka) below. Ultimately a compound of 四(よ) (yo, “four”) + 日(か) (-ka, counter for days).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Considered to be the old form of 四日(よっか) (yokka), but the earliest kana attestations are instead ようか (youka, see below) in works like the Kagerō Nikki, which may be the older form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly the older form of 四日(よか) (yoka) above. The shift to yoka ~ yokka may have been to avoid homophony with 八日(ようか) (yōka < yauka, “eight days”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 図(と)書(しょ) (tosho, “books”) + 館(かん) (-kan, “building”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from older unattested 男(を)人(ひと) (wofito), synchronically analyzable as a compound of 男(を) (wo → o, “male, man”) + 人(ひと) (fito → hito, “person”).
Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *wopitə, with many Ryukyuan cognates.
First attested in roughly 1220.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712.
Cognate with 端 (tsuma, “edge, side of something”), from the sense of "person by one's side".
Generally spelled 夫 in reference to a husband and 妻 in reference to a wife.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 奥様(おくさま) (okusama); equivalent to 奥(おく) (oku) + さん (san).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kiraɸi/ → /kirawi/ → /kirai/
From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 嫌(きら)う (kirau, “to detest, dislike, hate”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears starting from the Muromachi period (室(むろ)町(まち)時(じ)代(だい) (Muromachi jidai), c. 1336–1573).
Derived as the -na adjective construction of -i adjective 小(ちい)さい (chīsai, “small, little”), which see for more.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nipa/ → /nifa/ → /niwa/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ko₂ko₂ro₂⟩ → */kəkərə/ → /kokoro/
From Old Japanese 心 (ko₂ko₂ro₂), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kəkərə. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Compare Okinawan 心 (kukuru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
Cognate with 裏 (ura, “inside”) and 浦 (ura, “inlet”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/simʉ/ → */ɕimʉ/ → /ɕiɴ/
From Middle Chinese 心 (MC sim).
The Buddhist sense is a translation of Pali and Sanskrit चित्त (citta).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 下二段 (shimo nidan) verb 捨つ (sutsu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 捨つ entry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yəkə. Cognate with Kunigami 横 (ゆく゚ー, yukū), Miyako 横 (ゆく, yuku), Northern Amami Ōshima 横 (ゆく゚, yuxu), Okinawan 横 (ゆく, yuku), Yaeyama 横 (ゆく, yuku), Yonaguni 横 (どぅぐ, dugu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 橫 (MC hwaeng, “horizontal”) and 橫 (MC hwaengH, “violent; unexpected”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 歯(は) (ha, “tooth”) + 医者(いしゃ) (isha, “doctor”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, derived from 音 (na, “(emotional) sound, voice”, bound form) + く (-ku, verb suffix). Cognate with 鳴(な)く (naku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the classical upper bigrade verb (バ行上二段活用) 浴ぶ, possibly from Old Japanese 浴む (amu), in the 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.
Cognate with Okinawan 浴みゆん (amiyun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/manɡwa/ → /manɡa/
Coined in Japan of Middle Chinese‐derived elements, as a compound of 漫(まん) (man, “as one pleases”) + 画(が) (ga, “picture”).
The sense of a drawing first appears in 1798 in the foreword to Santō Kyōden's picture book 四(し)時(じの)交(ゆき)加(かい) (Shiji no Yukikai), already using the modern shinjitai spelling of 漫画.
The archaic sense of “Eurasian spoonbill” is attested even earlier in the 1778 medical text 薬(やく)品(ひん)手(て)引(びき)草(ぐさ) (Yakuhin Tebikigusa).
In the late nineteenth century, the term was repurposed as a translation for the English word caricature. This shift was led by artists such as Imaizumi Ippyō and Kitazawa Rakuten to elevate satirical drawings (formerly known as ポンチ絵(え) (ponchi-e)) into a professional art form. It later expanded to encompass sequential “comics” as that medium gained popularity in the early twentieth century.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 灰 (hai, “ash”) + 皿 (sara, “plate”). The sara changes to zara as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 熱 (MC nyet).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pako/ → /fako/ → /hako/
From Old Japanese pako. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *pako.
This term originally referred to a kind of wicker basket or box introduced from continental Asia, and the word is thought to be a borrowing from, or cognate with, a predecessor form of modern Korean 바구니 (baguni, “basket”). Compare Middle Korean 바고니〮 (pàkwòní).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Originally referred to new buds and shoots, later expanding via metonymy to mean green.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ipu/ → /iɸu/ → /*iwu/ → /iu/ → /juː/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ipu.
Medial /p/ regularly changed from [p] → [ɸ] → [w]. Japanese never distinguished between /wu/ and /u/, so that automatically becomes [u]. The /w/ only surfaces in the negative form of iwanai, where the phoneme sequence /wa/ exists. Surface forms /iwimasu/ and /iwemasu/ automatically became /iimasu/ and /iemasu/ since Japanese no longer distinguishes /wi, we/ from /i, e/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From し (shi, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb する (suru, “to do”)) + 合(あ)い (ai, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 合(あ)う (au, “to do to each other; to do together”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 贈(おく)る (okuru) + 物(もの) (-mono)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, in turn from Proto-Japonic *karu. In Old Japanese, seldom used outside of proper nouns, where in the Kojiki it is spelled as 加流 and in the Man'yōshū it is spelled as 軽, suggesting that this word was already used in Old Japanese with the meaning "light, lightweight". This might be weakly strengthened by a kana annotation of 軽 as karu(ku) in the Nihon Shoki.
It is generally believed that karu(si) was the older form; this is also supported by Ryukyuan cognates (see Proto-Ryukyuan *karu). In the Heian period and Kamakura period, the variant かろし (karoshi) → かろい (karoi) has started to be in use, while 軽し (karushi) → 軽い (karui) has still seldom usage.
Later, both karosi and karusi began to be used in parallel. Then, in Early Modern Japanese, karui slowly began to replace karoi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Modern form of Old Japanese adjective あをし (awosi); from Old Japanese awo-, from Proto-Japonic *awo.
⟨awosi⟩ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → ⟨awoki₁⟩ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /aoi/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)
